Cottage Chaos - 10 years on

By: Nicky Troll | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
From small beach cottages to palace-like properties – all illegal, all devastating the Eastern Cape coast line.

Summary:
10 years after our first stories on illegal beach cottage – it’s still a free for all! Seaside plots no longer go for a bottle of brandy and R200, you’re looking at about R15 000 for your piece of illegal paradise.
We go undercover shopping for a plot and take to sky to capture the destruction.
Despite three pieces of active legislation protecting our coastline - why is nothing being done to these rich squatters?

Further information:
In the last 5 years, at least 60 new properties have been built in the Umgazana region in the Eastern Cape. 17 of these owners have been issued with notices to demolish, but these wealthy squatters have lawyered up and are dragging out the legal process despite being on the wrong side of the law.
They have built roads through mangroves, destroyed sand dunes, and forestry to get their perfect spot.
Rumour has it that even an MP has bought and illegal plot in paradise.
The Sand mine on the dune in Umgazana is believed to be the biggest on the Eastern Cape Coast. The sand is being used not only for illegal properties, but for schools and low cost housing projects in the area.
UNDERCOVER OPERATION
- We meet with the local chiefs to find out about buying a plot.
- We go in search of illegal sand mining operations and try to find the sellers and buyers of the sand.
AERIAL FOOTAGE
- We have photos and footage dating back to 1960 of the very coast line that now is starting to resemble built-up Balito.
HISTORY
In our earlier stories we featured Bruce Houston’s illegal cottage – 10 years later the case is only being finalised now.
WHO IS TO BLAME?
Environmental Affairs in the Eastern Cape are doing on the leg work, issuing notices, building cases against illegal occupiers, but when they hand over to the Department of Justice – nothing seems to happen.

Sources to be interviewed on the record

- UNDERCOVER – Chief
- UNDERCOVER – Sand Miners
- ILLEGAL OCCUPIERS & THEIR LEGAL REPRESENTATION
- DEPARTMENT OF ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS
- BATELUERS PILOT THAT HAS BEEN FLYING THE REGION FOR 10 years
- DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE








Extra Budget Items:
I'd have to a trip down Umgazana before we take crew down to the undercover. It would require a flight to Umtata, car hire and accommodation for two nights (it's cheap down there :) ) I won't charge for my time, it's part of the story.

Press Release:


The holiday is over
Ten years ago wealthy holidaymakers secured properties along the pristine Eastern Cape coastline in exchange for a bottle of brandy and R200. These plots remain a bargain, but today will set you back anything from R5 000 to R20 000. Over 30 beach front properties have sprung up on these prime pieces of land in the Umgazana region, despite active legislation that aims to protect this sensitive coastline. Carte Blanche asks: why are these illegal cottage owners not being brought to book?


Script:


STRUCTURE

VO: In 2005, we brought you the story of illegal beach cottages on the Wild Coast - the battle to demolish structures and bring the culprits to book.

UPSOUND DIV: …. That will be the end of the wild coast, it will be total, total devastation…

VO: At the time, the illegal cottage owners went the legal route because they believed they had a right to be there.

UPSOUND Grenville: … it’s their land and the chief decide who to dish it out to….

VO: Ten years later those cottages still stand, along with even more built on the Wild Coast says Eastern Cape Green Scorpions Director, Div de Villiers.

DIV: you’ve got everything from a tiny cottage, perhaps a mud hut right through to big mansions,
DEVI: How do people go put up structures on land that doesn’t belong to them legally?
DIV: It’s a chance that they take. // they’re prepared to fight it, get a good legal team behind them and then they can have a holiday that’s relatively inexpensive right on some of the prime beachfront property of South Africa.

VO: These days everyone wants a holiday spot on the Wild Coast.

DIV: it’s not only white people, you’ve got coloureds, Indians, across the board, everyone is grabbing a piece of land where they can.

VO: The Bateluers, who fly for the environment say they’ve seen the impact on the coastline first hand. Eastern Cape Pilot, Reid Wardle says new structures are constantly going up in certain hotspots.

REID: The lawless development that is going on now – is not on!

VO: One of the most affected areas is Mngazana – just 30km south of Port St John’s.

Despite no government permission granted, there have been at least 30 additional structures erected amongst existing legal cottages in recent years.

LINK: Prior to 1994, certain people were given permission to have beach cottages here, legal beach cottages in the former Transkei.

VO: In recent years no valid permission to occupy certificates were issued.

But that didn’t stop new people from moving in. Swiss national Rahel Heiri fell in love with the Wild Coast in 2010 and wanted to make it her home.

RAHEL: We thought it would be an amazing place to start a backpackers

VO: So Rahel started the traditional process of acquiring land in Lubanzi near Coffee Bay.

RAHEL: SO you need to go talk to the local community, you need to go talk to the headman you need their approval.

VO: After offering a share in her business and employment opportunities Rahel was welcomed into the community.

It’s a decade old process. Rumour has it that many traditional leaders traded pristine land for as little as R200 and a bottle of brandy.

The true dymanics of acquiring a piece of illegal paradise have never been exposed.

We went undercover, armed with hidden cameras and contacted a former headman from Mngazana.

UPSOUND PHONE CALL:
MPENDULO: we can now look for the place and call you the next day.// Maybe about 6 or 7000 like that.

VO: That and at least two cases of beer, two bottles of brandy and cold drink.

LINK: Not all traditional leaders are out to make a quick buck, who won’t sell, no matter.

FUNDILE: We don’t allow that this land should be sold, because we are leaving it for our descendants

VO: Fundile Masikantsi is a Headman at Mpande, just south of Mngazana – he believes the land is their heritage.

A heritage that is being destroyed in some parts like Brazen Head adjacent to Mngazana.

DIV: Look at the excavation that has taken place here, even if we demolish the structure how are we going to fix this up? All the forest is gone virtually.

VO: The next site is already beyond repair and the foundations are yet to be laid.

DIV: It’s going to take decades before you rehab - you’ve got to get the soil structure back, and rock and try and stabilize it and then get the forest to grow again

VO: No building is allowed within the 1-kilometer high watermark along the Wild Coast, it is a declared coastal conservation area and protected by three pieces of legislation.

Our undercover investigation, revealed that the Elders are aware of the environmental impacts.

They explained we’d have to build on a local land owner’s site that already had proper permission from government.

UNDERCOVER: it’s true now, A person must be under an (existing) resident because//, Nature, it doesn’t help that you are just giving it to them // because they will come back and complain about us // when Nature starts hassling them.

VO: Although it’s a loophole, it isn’t completely legal either.

DIV: They are still in contravention in terms of the land affairs laws and they are still messing up the environment

VO: That’s something Headmen, like Fundile, realize.

FUNDILE: We will never take the money // because it wont do anything for us,// because if we give them the land, we will be left with nothing, and that R10 000 will finish but the land doesn’t finish.

VO: In one section of Mngazana, we counted four half erected structures. Locals say this one belongs to a Bishop Sharpley’s family, he is a member of the Eastern Cape Legislature.

The Bishop claims that he lives in the area, and that he was born there, entitling him to a piece of paradise.

DEVI: You don’t have a right to be within the 1 kilometer high water mark
SHARPLEY: no, no, no, no, no, no…. //As a matter of fact, I think this entire environmental thing needs to be totally challenged

VO: He’s stopped construction pending an appeal, Bishop Sharpley, insists that the legislation being used is unconstitutional.

DIV: The Old Transkei Decree was shown in Court to be constitutional // and it was actually mentioned in the Supreme Court of Appeal that the Decree is constitutional and valid.

VO: Div says the legislation is clear and that there have been some breakthroughs.

DIV: but we have made progress, we have demolished more than a 100 houses along the Wild Coast

VO: Two weeks ago we accompanied the Green Scorpions on a joint operation with the police to Lubanzi where Rahel’s backpackers is located. It was D-day for five illegal cottages right on the sea.

Two of the cottage owners had died, another cottage was unclaimed, and owners of the remaining two hadn’t filed appeals with the minister. It seems the law is finally working for the environment.

LINK: This is the first time that section 60 of the integrated coastal management act has been used, to get rid of illegal structures on the wild coast – and the department says this first of more to come.

VO: Only community structures erected before 1992 are safe from the firing line. Although Rahel’s Backpackers was not on the demolition list that day - there is no guarantee that it won’t be next.

RAHEL: I still hope that we can keep up the talks and find a solution. // I understand that we need to move out of that – so if we have to move the backpackers, we will move it.

VO: She claims that the community didn’t tell her about the governmental process.

RAHEL: We are not regretting it, it has been an interesting path, I understand environmental affairs point of view that you cannot have an illegal development on the coast and I understand that holiday cottage and this can’t be allowed.

VO: The community watched as the illegal cottages were set alight and reduced to rubble which will be removed by government at a later stage.

Demolitions are a complicated process and it has taken three years to achieve.

DIV: The wheel turns slowly, as you’ve seen here in the Transkei, things happen slowly, but they happen eventually.

VO: Currently there are 60 civil cases pending, and another 20 criminal cases that have yet to make it to court.

Advocate Thuli Majova is from the Mthatha National Prosecuting Authority. So far only two criminal cases have gone to court and both resulted in wins for the state.

DEVI: Why is it taking so long?
THULI: When the docket at least comes statements from both departments should be there, including the municipality.
DEVI: And are they often missing?
THULI: Always, you will only find Environmental Affairs statement only.
DEVI: So are you saying the delays are not your fault?
THULI: They can not be... shakes head... never...

VO: It only leaves questions for the Department of Rural Development and Land Reform who share the responsibility with Environmental Affairs. But Lamahlubi Mbekeni denies that her department is holding up cases.

LAMAHLUBI: We have been members of the Wild Coast Task team – it can not be accurate that they have not received any response from us.

VO: Minutes of meetings they very rarely attend, show that documents from the Department of Rural Development remain outstanding.

We wanted to talk to traditional leaders – but our cameras weren’t welcome. An angry community member first chased us and then tried to prevent us from leaving, threatening violence.

UPSOUND SUGAR: Stay like that, we are going to fix it now

VO: He continued insisting that the land belonged to the community.

DEVI: Traditional leaders are saying no, no, no, this is our land – they believe that
LA: They do believe that, // if your forefathers have been in control of the same areas, and you are now in control as the current traditional leader, the belief would be that you own what ever you in control of.
DEVI: This is why taking so long – who has right to land – government one opinion, traditional leaders another.

VO: Rahel wants to do the right thing, she doesn’t want to steal her piece of paradise, she wants to be part of the community….

RAHEL: We want to stay in this village, we’ll have to find another property again together with the community and then get the proper permit from environmental affairs

VO: Looking after the wild coast is a responsibility embraced by Headmen like Fundile.

FUNDILE: We protect it because this place here is ours. // We were born here.// If we had to let this land be taken and sold by others, //it [the land] will be finished
DIV: If we are going to allow land grabs and people to continue building illegally - you’re just wrecking a piece of paradise.

PROMOS

PROMO 1
VO: Some traditional leaders and greedy land-grabbers try to dodge legislation, to make prime Wild Coast land their own.

DIV: it’s not only white people, you’ve got coloureds, Indians, across the board, everyone is grabbing a piece of land where they can.

PROMO 2
VO: The price for an illegal piece of paradise has gone up from a bottle of brandy and R200 to at least two cases of beer, two bottles of brandy, cold drink and a sizable cash payment.

MPENDULO: Maybe about 6 or 7000 like that.

VO: We investigate.

PROMO 3 – 10 seconds
VO: The holiday is over for some illegal beach cottages on the Wild Coast, leaving others wondering if they will be next.

VO: The holiday is over for self-proclaimed owners of illegal beach cottages built on the pristine Wild Coast.

RAHEL: I still hope that we can keep up the talks and find a solution.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): From small beach cottages to palace-like properties – all illegal, all devastating the Eastern Cape coast line.
metadata.Summary: 10 years after our first stories on illegal beach cottage – it’s still a free for all! Seaside plots no longer go for a bottle of brandy and R200, you’re looking at about R15 000 for your piece of illegal paradise. We go undercover shopping for a plot and take to sky to capture the destruction. Despite three pieces of active legislation protecting our coastline - why is nothing being done to these rich squatters?
metadata.Further information: In the last 5 years, at least 60 new properties have been built in the Umgazana region in the Eastern Cape. 17 of these owners have been issued with notices to demolish, but these wealthy squatters have lawyered up and are dragging out the legal process despite being on the wrong side of the law. They have built roads through mangroves, destroyed sand dunes, and forestry to get their perfect spot. Rumour has it that even an MP has bought and illegal plot in paradise. The Sand mine on the dune in Umgazana is believed to be the biggest on the Eastern Cape Coast. The sand is being used not only for illegal properties, but for schools and low cost housing projects in the area. UNDERCOVER OPERATION - We meet with the local chiefs to find out about buying a plot. - We go in search of illegal sand mining operations and try to find the sellers and buyers of the sand. AERIAL FOOTAGE - We have photos and footage dating back to 1960 of the very coast line that now is starting to resemble built-up Balito. HISTORY In our earlier stories we featured Bruce Houston’s illegal cottage – 10 years later the case is only being finalised now. WHO IS TO BLAME? Environmental Affairs in the Eastern Cape are doing on the leg work, issuing notices, building cases against illegal occupiers, but when they hand over to the Department of Justice – nothing seems to happen.
